dm: The Perfection of Patience
gm: Chapter Six: Teaching Patience

dm: Whatever virtuous deeds have been accumulated, Such as generosity and offerings to the Sugatas, Over a thousand eons, A single moment of anger destroys them all.
gm: Accumulated over a thousand eons, Generosity, offerings to the Sugatas, and so forth— Whatever good conduct there is, all of that, A single moment of anger destroys.

dm: There is no evil like hatred, And no austerity like patience. Therefore, one should diligently practice patience In various ways.
gm: There is no misdeed like hatred; There is no ascetic practice like patience. Therefore, earnestly upon patience, One should meditate in various ways.

dm: If one harbors a mind of stinging hatred, The mind will not experience the taste of peace; One will find neither joy nor happiness, Will not sleep, and will become unstable.
gm: If one holds a mind with the dart of hatred, The mind does not experience peace, Neither joy nor happiness is obtained, Sleep does not come, and one becomes unsteady.

dm: Even those who depend on a master's kindness, Having been provided for with wealth and honors, Will seek to kill that master If he is possessed by anger.
gm: Those who, through wealth and honors, Have been favored and depend upon him, Even they, against the hate-filled Master, will rebel to kill him.

dm: Because of that, his friends will become weary of him; Even if gathered through generosity, they will not remain. In short, there is no one at all Who dwells in happiness while possessed by anger.
gm: Because of it, friends become disheartened; Though gathered by generosity, they do not stay. In brief, an angry person who dwells in happiness— There is no such thing at all.

dm: The enemy of anger produces these And many other such sufferings. Those who strive to conquer anger Will find happiness in this life and the next.
gm: The enemy of anger will create These and other such sufferings. Whoever applies effort and destroys anger, That one is happy in this life and the next.

dm: Finding its fuel in the mental unease Caused by the occurrence of the unwanted And the obstruction of what is desired, Hatred flourishes and then destroys me.
gm: From doing what is undesired and Hindering what is desired, there arises Mental unhappiness; having found this food, Hatred grows strong and destroys me.

dm: Therefore, I shall utterly destroy The sustenance of that enemy; For this enemy has no function Other than to cause me harm.
gm: Therefore, of that enemy, I Shall completely destroy the food; For, other than harming me, This enemy has no other task.

dm: No matter what befalls me, I shall not allow my joyful mind to be disturbed; For even if I become unhappy, my desires will not be fulfilled, And my virtues will decline.
gm: Whatever happens, I Shall not disturb my joyful mind. Even if unhappy, what is desired is not accomplished, And virtues will decline.

dm: If there is a remedy for it, Why be unhappy about it? If there is no remedy for it, What is the use of being unhappy?
gm: If it can be remedied, What is the point of being unhappy about it? If it cannot be remedied, What use is there in being unhappy about it?

dm: For myself or for my friends, I do not desire suffering, contempt, harsh words, Or unpleasantness; But for an enemy, it is the opposite.
gm: For myself or my friends, Suffering, contempt, harsh words, And unpleasantness are not desired; For enemies, it is the opposite of that.

dm: The causes of happiness occur only occasionally, While the causes of suffering are extremely numerous. Without suffering, there is no renunciation; Therefore, O mind, remain steadfast.
gm: The causes of happiness occur sometimes; The causes of suffering are very many. Without suffering, there is no renunciation. Therefore, mind, resolve to be steadfast!

dm: The followers of Durgā and the people of Karṇapa Endure the sensations of being burned, cut, and so forth; Why then am I so cowardly, When my goal is liberation?
gm: Devotees of asceticism and the Karṇapas Endure the sensations of burning, cutting, and so forth Pointlessly; for the sake of liberation, Why am I cowardly?

dm: There is nothing whatsoever That does not become easy through habituation. Therefore, by habituating yourself to minor harms, Learn to endure great adversity.
gm: That which does not become easier through familiarity— There is no such thing at all. Therefore, by becoming familiar with small harms, Endure great harms!

dm: Why do you not see the meaningless suffering Caused by snakes, gadflies, and the like, By sensations such as hunger and thirst, And by afflictions such as skin rashes?
gm: From snakes and gadflies, Sensations of hunger, thirst, and so forth, And conditions like rashes and so forth— Why have I not seen pointless sufferings?

dm: Against heat, cold, rain, wind, and the like, And against sickness, bondage, beatings, and so forth, I shall not be sensitive or fragile; For if I am, the harm will only increase.
gm: Towards heat, cold, rain, wind, and so forth, Sickness, bondage, beatings, and so forth, I should not be overly sensitive; If I do so, the harm increases.

dm: Some, when they see their own blood, Become even more exceptionally brave and steadfast; Others, when they see the blood of another, Become dazed and faint.
gm: When some see their own blood, They become exceptionally brave and steadfast; When some see the blood of others, They faint and fall unconscious.

dm: This arises from whether the mind is steady Or whether it has fallen into a state of cowardice; Therefore, disregard all harm, And remain unassailable by sufferings.
gm: That is due to the steadfastness of the mind, Or due to a cowardly nature. Therefore, disregarding harms, Make yourself unaffected by sufferings!

dm: Even when suffering arises, The wise should not allow their mind to be disturbed. For in the battle against the afflictions, There is much harm during the fight.
gm: Even when suffering arises, the wise Should not cloud the clarity of the mind. When waging war with the afflictions, During battle, harms are many.

dm: Disregarding all suffering, To conquer the enemies of hatred and the like— These are the victorious heroes; The rest are merely slaying corpses.
gm: Having disregarded all sufferings, Those who conquer enemies such as anger— They are the victorious heroes; The rest slay corpses.

dm: Furthermore, the qualities of suffering are: Through weariness, it dispels arrogance, Compassion arises for those in cyclic existence, One avoids misdeeds and delights in virtue.
gm: Furthermore, the quality of suffering is That through sorrow, arrogance is dispelled, Compassion arises for those in cyclic existence, Sin is shunned, and virtue is delighted in.

dm: Since one does not feel anger toward the great sources of suffering Such as bile and the like, Why be angry with sentient beings? They too are all impelled by conditions.
gm: Towards bile and so forth, which are Great sources of suffering, without being angry, Why be angry at those with minds? They too are all incited by conditions.

dm: For example, just as this illness arises Even though it is not desired, So too do the afflictions forcibly arise Even though they are not desired.
gm: For example, even without wishing it, Just as this sickness arises, Likewise, even without wishing it, Afflictions forcefully arise.

dm: Without thinking, "I shall be angry," People spontaneously become angry; Without thinking, "I shall arise," Anger likewise arises.
gm: Even without thinking, "I shall get angry," People get angry without choice; Even without thinking, "I shall produce it," Anger likewise arises.

dm: All faults, as many as there are, And various kinds of misdeeds, All arise through the power of conditions; They do not possess any independence.
gm: All however many faults there are, and Various kinds of sins— All these arise from the power of conditions; They do not possess independence.

dm: Even those assembled conditions Have no intention to produce anything; And that which is produced by them Has no intention, "I am being produced."
gm: Even those assemblages of conditions Have no intention, "We shall produce." And that which is produced by them has no Intention, "I shall be produced."

dm: That which is desired as the "Primal Substance" And that which is imputed as the "Self," Do not arise by intentionally thinking, "I shall come into being."
gm: Whatever is asserted as the "Primary Matter," and Whatever is imputed as the "Self"— Thinking, "I myself shall arise," They do not purposefully arise.

dm: If it does not exist because it has not been born, Then at that time, what could have the desire to be born? Since it is always distracted by sense objects, It is also not something that could cease.
gm: If it does not exist prior to arising, At that time, what wishes to arise? Since it would be permanently distracted by objects, It would also never cease.

dm: If that self were permanent, It would clearly be inactive, like space. Even if it were to encounter other conditions, What could they do to something that is unchanging?
gm: If that self is permanent, Like space, it is evidently inactive. Even if it meets with other conditions, What can be done to the unchanging?

dm: If it remains as it was before even at the time of acting, Then what has the action done to it? What kind of connection could there be Such that one could say, "This is its action"?
gm: If even at the time of acting it remains as before, What did the action do to it? By saying, "This is its action," What connection could there be?

dm: In this way, everything is dependent on other factors, And because of those factors, it lacks independence. Knowing this, one will not become angry At any phenomena, which are like magical illusions.
gm: Thus, everything is under the power of others, And that which has power is itself powerless. Having understood this, one will not get angry Towards all things, which are like emanations.

dm: If you ask, "Who is there to prevent what? Even the act of prevention is not reasonable," It is not unreasonable to desire the cessation Of sufferings that arise in dependence upon that.
gm: "By what is what to be reversed? Reversing too is illogical," if one says; In dependence upon that, the wish for sufferings' Continuum to be severed is not illogical.

dm: Therefore, whether it be an enemy or a friend, Should you see them acting improperly, Reflect that "This has arisen from such conditions," And in that way, remain at ease.
gm: Therefore, whether it is an enemy or a friend, If I see them doing what is improper, Thinking, "This arose from such conditions," I will remain happy, reflecting in this way.
